$comment: MCP HUB TEMPLATE. Copy the `mcpServers` block into your harness config (Claude Code reads ~/.claude.json). It ships pointing at a public hub anyone can sign up for, so a fresh clone can actually reach one; see `$hubUrl`. It is still a TEMPLATE: the token is yours and is never written here, and the hub is a default rather than a lock-in -- see `$bringYourOwnHub`. Nothing here is secret and nothing here should become secret -- see `$auth` below.
$hubUrl: The default is https://synapse.onedroid.ai/agent/mcp -- Synapse. Sign up at https://synapse.onedroid.ai; the vendor states one account covers Synapse and Engram and is free for individuals and small teams. This template is the same wiring the vendor's own quickstart prints: https://docs.onedroid.ai/quickstart. THE PATH IS THE PART PEOPLE GET WRONG. There are two auth avenues and each has its own URL: a personal access token uses /agent/mcp with NO hub slug, because the token is bound to a hub when you create it and the server resolves it from that; browser OAuth uses /hub/<slug>/mcp, where the slug is what selects the hub. Getting this backwards is the most common wiring mistake -- a token sent to /hub/<slug>/mcp fails with ERR_SCOPE_UNAVAILABLE unless the slug happens to match, and there is no reason to prefer that form for a token client. This config is the token avenue, so it is /agent/mcp. Full explanation, including why the asymmetry is real rather than arbitrary: https://docs.onedroid.ai/endpoints
$bringYourOwnHub: You can bring your own hub -- the default is a default, not a requirement. Replace the `url` with your own MCP endpoint and rename the server key to match the hub it points at. Your provider tells you the exact path; do not assume it takes the same shape as the one above, which is specific to how Synapse separates token auth from OAuth. The method also works with no hub at all: delete this file and you lose shared memory and connectors, nothing else.
$auth: The token is written as ${DF_HUB_TOKEN}, an ENVIRONMENT REFERENCE, not the token itself. Two reasons, and the second is the one people learn the hard way. (1) A config file gets copied, committed, screenshotted and pasted into issues; an env var does not travel with it -- the vendor's own guidance is a password manager or secret store, never chat, git, or a shared doc. (2) Auth is therefore INHERITED FROM THE ENVIRONMENT, so a headless or scheduled run reaches the hub only if that variable is exported in the process that spawned it -- otherwise the child boots cleanly, fails every write, and keeps going. Export it in your shell profile, and check it is set before launching anything unattended. `df-preflight` checks exactly this and reports it as its own finding class. Minting, scoping, rotating and revoking a token: https://docs.onedroid.ai/tokens
$naming: Name each server for the hub it points at, not for the tools behind it. The tool list changes whenever you connect or disconnect an upstream; the hub does not. Add one object per hub if you use more than one -- separate hubs stay separate, and a single merged hub is how content crosses a boundary you meant to keep.
$verify: After filling this in, prove it works before relying on it: `python3 boot-kit/scripts/df-preflight.py --report` makes a live tools/list call against every configured hub. A present Authorization header proves nothing -- tokens expire, and an expired one looks identical to a working one until something needs it.
